deep.reconstruction:
This page closes Corollary 3 and gives Scholion 2 with the first part of a table; the table continues on the next page. The problem served: for each prime P = 4n+1, describe all integers a with P | a²+1, so that later the primality or factorisation of large numbers of the form aa+1 can be studied.

The rule from the preceding pages works as follows. Write P = p² + q², which Euler says is always possible and in only one way. Run the Euclidean algorithm on p and q; the quotients generate continued-fraction convergents. Combine the last convergents to get a number a (for example a = 1·p + 0·1 = p when q = 1, or a = 2p − 1 when q = p − 1). Then the general solution of P | a²+1 is a = mP ± a₀.

In modern terms, a₀ ≡ p·q⁻¹ (mod P). It is one of the two square roots of −1 modulo P, and the solution set of x² ≡ −1 (mod P) is exactly {±a₀}. The continued fraction is simply Euler's way of inverting q modulo P. For example, 29 = 2² + 5²: 2⁻¹ ≡ 15 (mod 29), so 5·15 = 75 ≡ 17 ≡ −12, matching the table's a = 29m ± 12.

The page finishes Corollary 3 for the prime 2: every odd square plus one is even. Scholion 2 then states that Euler treated every prime 4n+1 this way. The table on this page covers primes up to 97 (2, 5, 13, …, 97), each with its two-square decomposition and residue ±a₀.

I checked every residue on this page:
- 2² + 1 = 5
- 5² + 1 = 26 = 2·13
- 4² + 1 = 17
- 12² + 1 = 145 = 5·29
- 6² + 1 = 37
- 9² + 1 = 82 = 2·41
- 23² + 1 = 530 = 10·53
- 11² + 1 = 122 = 2·61
- 27² + 1 = 730 = 10·73
- 34² + 1 = 1157 = 13·89
- 22² + 1 = 485 = 5·97

All are correct.
errors: The first row reads '2 = 1² + 2²' in both the transcription and, as far as can be read, the scan. It should be 2 = 1² + 1², as the previous page itself states (2 = 1+1, p = q = 1). This is a printing or transcription slip; the value a = 2m ± 1 is correct.
Uniqueness of the two-square representation is asserted here without proof. Euler handled it in his separate papers on sums of two squares, so it is not a gap within this paper's logic.

ideas.what: Square root of −1 mod p obtained from the representation p = x² + y² as x·y⁻¹ mod p, with the inverse computed by the Euclidean algorithm / continued fractions
ideas.modern_name: square root of −1 modulo p from a sum-of-two-squares representation (the converse direction of the Hermite–Serret / Cornacchia algorithm)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore; this E283 table is a known instance. The reverse direction is credited to Hermite and Serret (1848) and to Cornacchia (1908).
ideas.where_published: E283, Novi Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae 9 (published 1764)

ideas.what: Every prime 4n+1 is a sum of two squares in exactly one way
ideas.where_published: E228 and related papers on sums of two squares

ideas.what: Table of the residues a mod p with p | a²+1, for primes p ≡ 1 mod 4
ideas.modern_name: table of roots of x² ≡ −1 (mod p)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E283); later tables by Gauss, Jacobi (Canon arithmeticus) and Cunningham

deep.surprise_reason: This is a correct, routine table that is already known as part of E283. The method (square root of −1 from a two-square representation via the Euclidean algorithm) is standard, and nothing on the page is uncredited.
transcription_corrections: The first table row should read '2 = 1² + 1²'. Whether the print has 1² + 2² (an original misprint) or the scan is ambiguous, the mathematically correct form is 1² + 1².
